questions.question: Transition vs animation — the properties, the performance rules, and when do you reach for each?
questions.title: Transitions Vs Animations
questions.direct_answer: TRANSITION = a one-shot, state-change-driven interpolation: you change a property (class swap, hover, JS style write) and the browser animates FROM old TO new over duration with an easing — great for feedback (hover, open/close, toggle). ANIMATION = a keyframe timeline (@keyframes with % stops, iteration-count, direction, fill-mode, play-state) that runs INDEPENDENTLY of state changes — loops, multi-step sequences, entrance choreography. The performance law for BOTH: animate ONLY transform and opacity (compositor-only — no layout, no paint; animating top/left/width/height forces layout every frame). The control split: transitions start automatically on property change; animations need the trigger condition (class, animation-play-state) and can pause/loop; JS-driven values prefer WAAPI (element.animate) over CSS for imperative cases.

Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SC[state change: class hover JS] --> TR[transition — one-shot tween]
    TL[timeline: loops, steps, entrance] --> AN[animation + keyframes]
    TO[transform + opacity] --> COMP[compositor only — 60fps safe]
    LP[top left width height] --> LAY[layout every frame — jank]
    BP[background color] --> PAIN[repaint per frame]
    WC[will-change: transform] --> PROMOTE[pre-promote layer — sparingly]
    JS[js-driven motion] --> WAAPI[element.animate + finished promise]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The easing vocabulary (the difference between amateur and polished): linear (mechanical — avoid for UI); ease-out (fast-then-slow — the UI default: things ARRIVE, feels responsive); ease-in (slow-then-fast — things LEAVE, exit/dismiss); the cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) family is the 'standard ease-out' of most design systems; overshoot curves (back/elastic) for playful entrances. The rule of thumb: enter with ease-out, exit with ease-in, move between with a symmetric ease — plus prefers-reduced-motion: reduce to collapse them to near-zero (an a11y REQUIREMENT, not an option).

The fill-mode and reversibility semantics (where transitions beat naive animations): a transition is automatically REVERSIBLE — remove the class and it tweens BACK along the same curve; an animation with forwards keeps its end state (or both for back-fill). This reversibility is why hover/press states should be transitions, and why a nav-drawer built with an animation needs explicit close logic (the class-swap pattern handles it with one transition declaration). animation-play-state: paused is the pause-without-reset (spinners, background motion); animations on :hover restart each entry (the animation-restart gotcha).

The orchestration layer (the scale answers): animation-delay chains steps (a stagger: nth-child delays — the list-entrance idiom), @starting-style (the 2023+ answer for 'animate the INITIAL state' — transitionable entry for elements that had no prior state, closing the last gap between display:none mounts and animation); View Transitions API (document.startViewTransition — the browser snapshots old/new and cross-fades MORPHS between them: page-level choreography with ~3 lines, the successor to hand-rolled FLIP); and scroll-driven animations (animation-timeline: scroll()/view() — progress tied to scroll position, no JS scroll listeners, the newest primitive). Name those three and the answer reads current.
